METHOD GUIDE

How the analysis works

The app samples frames from a tank video, finds candidate fish centers, measures distances between those centers, and connects nearby detections into groups. Every result depends on what the detector found in that frame.

01 / FRAMES

Which frames are analyzed?

The browser reads the selected video at the chosen interval, 200 milliseconds by default. That gives about five sampled frames per second. A crop restricts detection to the selected tank area; exported coordinates still refer to the original video frame. You can draw a crop on the preview or enter its coordinates. Background mode can follow provisional fish paths between samples up to 250 ms apart. T numbers label these paths, not verified individual identities. A fish can exchange identities with another during an overlap.

02 / DETECTION

Background subtraction

This is the default method for a fixed camera and a relatively stable tank background.

  1. Build a reference. Sample up to 25 moments across the video and take the median grayscale value at each pixel. Moving fish usually disappear from this median image.
  2. Find foreground changes. In each analyzed frame, mark pixels at least 24 grayscale levels darker than the reference. In marked dark regions, accept brighter changes of the same size too, so pale fish remain visible against a dark floor. Use the preview’s area tool to mark dark and light areas with rectangles or four corners; the last drawn region wins at overlaps. Results and exports classify each fish by its center as dark, light, or unmarked. With one fish expected and a marked dark region, the rest of the usable tank counts as light, and the timeline shows light/dark changes instead of group changes. Missing or uncertain positions appear as unknown; observed crossings require adjacent known samples. Four-corner tank outlines exclude pixels outside the angled swimming area. By default, dark-region candidates also need a small core beyond the learned background brightness range, allowing two pixels of fixture movement; this reduces ridge flicker while preserving a crossing fish’s full detected outline. Turn off Learn background flicker in Advanced settings if faint fish are missed. Small erosion and dilation passes remove specks and join nearby marked pixels. For rectangular crops, strips near crop edges are excluded to reduce tank-wall detections. Four-corner crops use their outlined boundary.
  3. Keep plausible regions. Connected marked pixels become candidate regions. The detector keeps regions with an area of 45–2,500 pixels and a span of at least 10 pixels. The reported position is the mean X and Y of the region’s marked pixels.
  4. Try to recover missed fish. When fewer candidates than the entered known fish count are found, the detector checks closer to the crop edges. It may also split a large region into two if fish appear joined. These attempts are flagged in the export; the known count does not force a correct result.

With one fish expected, a clear single detection also checks competing candidates in the immediately preceding sampled frame, including rejected candidates. A supported candidate within 45 pixels is selected if it is at least 8 pixels closer than the next candidate. Samples must be no more than 250 ms apart. The earlier frame’s center, tracking, measurements, and exports update together. This can change an earlier automatic choice; it does not infer hidden positions or work backward through a run of ambiguous frames. Reanalyze to apply this rule to an existing recording.

If no fish is found in a single-fish dark-region sample, the detector can search near supported candidates in the preceding 250 ms, including rejected alternatives. It can retain fainter connected body pixels, but requires a stronger core beyond the learned background range, compatible body size, and a new center within 45 pixels. Crop boundaries and reflection masks still apply. If a faint detection suddenly shrinks below half the preceding observed body, a tighter search can also recover connected body pixels near that earlier center. The new outline must retain the original fragment and pass brightness and size checks. These are measurements from the current image; a nearby detection alone cannot fill an empty frame.

Best suited to stationary footage. Reflections can look like fish, while overlapping fish can merge into one region. The median reference can also be inaccurate if a fish stays in one place for much of the video.

03 / DETECTION

Roboflow model

The optional method runs a trained Roboflow model in the browser on the selected crop. The app keeps predictions labeled as fish (or predictions without a label), requires a valid position inside the crop, and applies the chosen minimum confidence. The reported position is the center coordinate provided for the model’s bounding box. The app then adds the crop offset so it matches the original video frame.

The default project setting points to zebrafish_in_aquarium/9. This option needs the model assets and a publishable key. Its missed boxes and false boxes affect all later measurements. The known fish count is only used by background subtraction.

04 / MEASUREMENT

From pixels to inches

All spacing uses straight-line distance between detection centers: horizontal and vertical pixel differences are combined with the Pythagorean formula. To express that distance in inches, enter how many pixels span one 0.5-inch square of the paper grid.

pixels per inch= 2 × pixels per 0.5-inch squaredistance in inches= center distance in pixels ÷ pixels per inch

You can also click Draw calibration line below the preview, drag along a known distance, enter its actual length in inches, and click Use this scale. The app divides the line’s length in original-video pixels by its length in inches and fills in the equivalent half-inch-square calibration. Existing distance results update without rerunning detection. Measuring several squares near the swimming area helps reduce endpoint error.

For the prefilled 15.3 pixels per half-inch square, one inch is about 30.6 pixels. A 1.5-inch close distance therefore links centers up to 45.9 pixels apart. Recalibrate for other footage or camera views. Perspective makes a single scale approximate when fish appear at different depths.

05 / CLUSTERING

How groups are counted

For one frame, the app checks every pair of detection centers. It draws a link when their distance is at or below the chosen close distance. Fish connected directly or through other fish belong to one group. A group of two or more counts as a cluster; a single unlinked detection counts as isolated.

ABC

In this example, A and C can be farther apart than the close distance and still be in the same group through B. The smallest distance that makes every detected fish one group is the longest link needed to connect them all, not the largest pair distance.

What the displays mean

  • Colored dots and numbers: group membership within the selected frame. Group numbers do not identify the same fish or group in later frames.
  • Group sizes: a pattern such as 3+2 means two groups containing three and two detections.
  • Timeline marks: a mark appears when the sorted group-size pattern changes between sampled frames. A mark can also reflect a missed or extra detection.
  • Distance chart: shows how the selected frame’s cluster and isolated counts change as the link distance changes. Moving its slider recalculates grouping without running detection again.
06 / INTERPRETATION

How to check a result

First inspect the colored centers on the video. Count visible fish and check whether each center lands on one fish. Then inspect frames around timeline changes; a brief count change may be a merged fish or reflection. Finally, move the close-distance slider slightly. If the group count changes with a tiny adjustment, that frame sits near the chosen boundary.

After analysis, the Results workspace shows groups, measurements, and corrections together. Enable Edit centers to start from the current detections; click a center to remove it or an empty position to add one. You can show the automatic centers for comparison, mark frames reviewed, and export your marks and frame-level counts. To correct a frame, check all its centers and choose “Done & next” to apply and continue, or “Apply & stay” to inspect the updated measurements. Draft edits do not affect measurements until applied. This replaces its centers in measurements and exports; applying no marks sets its count to zero. “Restore automatic centers” undoes the change. Original automatic candidates remain in JSON and in the diagnostic comparison. Corrections affect only this frame; they do not rerun tracking. Distances and groups otherwise include uncertain estimated positions. The full-frame toggle lets you mark fish outside the analyzed crop; these are exported separately and excluded from the cluster comparison. Include crowded, isolated, reflection, and crop-edge cases. A matching fish count alone can hide a misplaced detection.

“Average pair distance” is the mean of all center-to-center pairs in each frame, averaged over frames with at least two detections. “Detections near another” is the share whose nearest detected neighbor is within the close distance. The random-spacing comparison places the same number of points uniformly inside the unmasked part of the crop 399 times and compares each frame’s mean nearest-neighbor distance with those simulations. It is a per-frame reference, not proof that the whole video is statistically clustered; adjacent frames are related, and the random placements ignore fish size and tank behavior.

For a stronger validation, label a representative set of frames by hand. Compare detected counts, centers, and cluster assignments with those labels before interpreting the whole video.

07 / REFLECTION MASKS

Fish above the floor and reflection masks

The crop is a boundary in the camera image, not a boundary on the tank floor. Include the space where fish swim, including fish appearing beyond the floor edge. In the preview, choose “Mask reflection area” and outline reflections or fixtures using rectangle or four-corner mode, then analyze again. Red masks apply to every sampled frame and to either detection method. They also exclude real fish that swim into them; a fixed mask cannot separate a fish and reflection in the same image area.

Human marks inside masks remain exportable but are excluded from automatic comparisons. The random-spacing reference uses only the unmasked portion of the crop. JSON settings include mask shapes and their corners.

08 / SHARPNESS DIAGNOSTICS

Can blur identify reflections?

Candidate labels can show an S score: higher values usually mean sharper local edges. The score is the variance of a Laplacian edge filter on original grayscale pixels around the candidate, with three pixels of padding. It is not a probability or a 0–100 scale. Real fish can be blurred by motion or focus, and reflections can be sharp. Contrast, noise, and the paper grid can also affect scores.

In Results, open “Diagnostics: fish & reflections” to label individual candidates, inspect local contrast, compare median scores across frames, and export the comparison CSV. These labels do not filter detections or change measurements. Leave suspected reflection areas unmasked for a diagnostic run so those candidates can be scored. An asterisk marks a patch clipped by the crop or a mask; a dash means a score is unavailable.

09 / OPTIONAL CANDIDATE SELECTION

Prefer candidates near the tank center

Background mode can keep the candidates nearest the middle of the selected crop when there are more than the known fish count. Before this selection, unusually large central regions are checked for a touching pair even when reflections have already filled the candidate count. A dagger (†) marks an estimated split; inspect both centers against the video. Splitting is based on region size and geometry and can still mistake a large single fish for a pair. Smaller overlaps can be supported by two stable dark bodies or a complete, non-estimated sample from the preceding 250 ms. Tracking can carry established paths through a short overlap, up to one second after an observed center. Estimates are flagged with dashed rings and † and never renew that deadline; they cannot reveal a fully hidden fish’s exact position. The final center selection leaves frames with fewer or exactly the known count unchanged. The option is off by default: a real fish at the edge can be farther out than a reflection.

Excluded candidates are marked with pink crosses and remain available in human review, the sharpness comparison CSV, and JSON. Distances and groups use only the kept candidates. The random-spacing percentile is omitted when the rule removes candidates or a kept center uses a temporal overlap estimate. Choosing central points can itself make spacing look artificially tight, and estimated positions should not be treated as directly observed.
